newsitem.title: BELGIUM: DOLLAR, OIL PRICE HIKES TO SPARK BELGIAN CPI SHOCK.
newsitem.headline: DOLLAR, OIL PRICE HIKES TO SPARK BELGIAN CPI SHOCK.

text.p: Inflation in Belgium looks set to increase in the months ahead as a rising dollar forces up the cost of imports, most notably petrol and foreign travel.

Analysts polled by Reuters said on Wednesday that the consumer price index could shoot up by 2.2 percent in August compared with August a year ago, a sharp accelaration from the 1.89 percent year-on-year inflation rate seen in July.

Some analysts predicted that inflation over the year as a whole would rise to above two percent, advancing to 2.7 or 2.8 percent in 1998, upsetting forecasts by the government, the European Union and the OECD think-tank.
News of Belgian petrol prices reaching all-time highs have fanned analysts' reviews of their forecasts.
Energy constitutes around seven percent of the inflation index. Mineral products, usually priced in dollars, account for just under nine percent of Belgian imports.
"A rise in the dollar by one franc means fuel prices go up by 20 centimes," the Belgian Petroleum Federation said.
It noted the share of the dollar in the cost of oil is limited to some 18 percent with the bulk of the remainder -- 70 percent -- made up of taxes and excise duties.
Nevertheless, economists said the dollar's seemingly inexorable rise was assuming worrying proportions.
"The dollar is the most fundamental factor," one said.
The greenback's advance picked up pace in recent weeks. In the last weeks it rose 8.5 percent on the Belgian franc, taking the gain for the year so far to 22.6 percent.
Analyst Caroline Ven at Kredietbank said the higher dollar would increase August's inflation to 2.3 percent, with the figure for the year as a whole seen at 2.2 or 2.3 percent.

However, the dollar would slip to around 35 Belgian francs next year and thus the upward pressure on inflation would ease in the second half of 1998, she said, noting also there was no pressure from Belgian wage costs since they were under control.
The oil price effect would only be temporary. She said oil prices would fall again, especially if the speculation that Iraqi oil might soon re-enter the market proved correct.
Analysts said a combination of factors, including the dollar, boosted oil prices
-- a decline in U.S. gasoline stocks;
-- the interruption of some 175,000 barrels a day of Colombian crude supplies after a key pipeline was blown up twice and partially destroyed by a landslide at the weekend;
-- a seasonal increase in petrol use in the summer holiday period in western Europe.
Analyst Guy Verfaille at Generale Bank said the oil effect could push Belgian inflation to 2.1 percent or more in August.

Long-term inflation forecasts would have to be revised up. Those for 1997, currently at 1.9 percent, would pass the two percent mark, 1998 estimates of 2.4 percent could rise to 2.7 or 2.8 percent if the dollar remained at this level, he said.
Petercam's Geert Noels said, though, that due to tough retail competition in Belgium, the overall oil and U.S. currency effect on inflation would be muted.
Analysts noted the dollar strength was threatening to raise the cost of foreign travel, affecting jet fuel prices, but also the price of airline tickets in Belgian francs.
In June and July the Economics Ministry, which publishes the inflation data, already singled out foreign travel as one of the factors behind rising inflation.
Analysts said the effect of the more costly dollar on Belgium's foreign currency debt would be limited since dollar-denominated debt amounted to only 0.62 percent of the total.
